es.a1.title: Your Spanish foundations
es.a1.identities.title: Who we are
es.a1.identities.can_do: I can introduce myself and describe where people are from.
es.a1.identities.guide: Use ser to identify people and describe their origin: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son. Spanish often leaves out the subject pronoun because the verb ending identifies it. Nationality adjectives normally begin with a lowercase letter and agree with the person they describe.

es.a1.classroom.title: A classroom in Spanish
es.a1.classroom.can_do: I can describe a classroom using articles and adjective agreement.
es.a1.classroom.guide: Nouns have grammatical gender. Articles and most descriptive adjectives agree in gender and number: el libro rojo → los libros rojos; la mesa pequeña → las mesas pequeñas. Adjectives ending in -e often use the same form for both genders: interesante. Use hay for what exists in a place.

es.a1.timetable.title: Your school day
es.a1.timetable.can_do: I can describe my school timetable using present-tense verbs and clock times.
es.a1.timetable.guide: Regular verbs use different endings for -ar, -er and -ir. Remove the infinitive ending and add the form that matches the subject. For clock times, use a la una and a las dos/tres. Days of the week begin with a lowercase letter.

es.a1.routines.title: Habits and routines
es.a1.routines.can_do: I can explain my daily routine using reflexive verbs and sequence words.
es.a1.routines.guide: Reflexive verbs use a pronoun that agrees with the subject: me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos, os levantáis, se levantan. Put it before a conjugated verb. Some everyday verbs are irregular: ir → voy; hacer → hago; tener → tengo. Sequence a routine with primero, después and al final.

es.a2.title: Tell stories. Connect ideas.
es.a2.past-events.title: Tell the story
es.a2.past-events.can_do: I can recount completed events using the pretérito indefinido.
es.a2.past-events.guide: Use the pretérito indefinido for events presented as finished in a completed time frame: ayer, la semana pasada. Regular -ar endings are -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron. For -er/-ir use -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. Written accents distinguish hablo (I speak) from habló (he/she spoke). Ir and ser share fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron.

es.a2.past-background.title: Set the scene
es.a2.past-background.can_do: I can distinguish background descriptions from events in a past-tense story.
es.a2.past-background.guide: The imperfect describes past habits and background: antes estudiaba, hacía frío. The indefinido moves the story forward with bounded events: de repente sonó el teléfono. Regular imperfect endings: -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban; -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. The contrast depends on how the speaker presents the situation, not simply whether it lasted a long time.

es.a2.plans.title: Plans that matter
es.a2.plans.can_do: I can explain plans, obligations and reasons using infinitive constructions.
es.a2.plans.guide: Use ir a + infinitive for intentions and plans: voy a estudiar. Keep the second verb in the infinitive. Tener que + infinitive expresses obligation; hay que + infinitive is impersonal. With porque you give a reason. Para + infinitive expresses a purpose: estudio para aprobar.

es.a2.opinions.title: Give an opinion
es.a2.opinions.can_do: I can express preferences, compare options and give a reason for my opinion.
es.a2.opinions.guide: With gustar, the thing liked is the grammatical subject: me gusta la historia; me gustan los idiomas. Use más/menos … que for comparisons and tan … como for equality. Some comparative forms are irregular: bueno → mejor, malo → peor. Give reasons with porque, and contrast with pero.

es.b1.title: Understand. Explain. Discuss.
es.b1.summarising.title: Say what a text says
es.b1.summarising.can_do: I can summarise a text's main ideas in my own words without adding my opinion.
es.b1.summarising.guide: A summary selects the main ideas without retelling every detail or adding your own opinion. Introduce the topic with el texto trata de or el autor explica que. Use your own words, a clear order and usually the present tense when reporting a text. Distinguish a claim from its example and never invent information missing from the source.

es.b1.subjunctive.title: Wishes and recommendations
es.b1.subjunctive.can_do: I can express wishes and recommendations using que and the present subjunctive.
es.b1.subjunctive.guide: Many expressions of wishes, recommendations or evaluation use que + subjunctive when a second subject is introduced: quiero que participes; es importante que estudies. Regular present-subjunctive endings swap vowel patterns: hablar → hable, hables, hable, hablemos, habléis, hablen; comer → coma… Not every sentence with que takes the subjunctive: creo que es útil normally uses the indicative.

es.b1.mediation.title: Help someone understand
es.b1.mediation.can_do: I can relay relevant information in Spanish for a specific recipient and purpose.
es.b1.mediation.guide: Mediation means selecting and explaining information for a particular person and purpose. It is not a word-for-word translation. Ask: what does the recipient need, what can be left out, and which cultural terms need explaining? Keep dates, conditions and obligations accurate. Use accessible Spanish and do not add claims that the source does not support.

es.b1.digital-life.title: Discuss digital life
es.b1.digital-life.can_do: I can discuss digital habits using reasons, examples and a counterargument.
es.b1.digital-life.guide: Build a short argument with a position, a reason and an example. Por un lado / por otro lado presents different aspects; sin embargo introduces a contrast; por eso presents a consequence. Do not treat a single example as proof of what always happens. Acknowledge a reasonable counterargument before giving your conclusion.

es.b2.title: Analyse and make your case
es.b2.text-analysis.title: From observation to analysis
es.b2.text-analysis.can_do: I can connect textual evidence to an interpretation of its effect on the reader.
es.b2.text-analysis.guide: An analysis explains how a text creates an effect. Connect an observation to evidence and interpretation: the author repeats a phrase; the repetition emphasises urgency; this may encourage the reader to act. Use careful language such as sugiere or puede transmitir when interpreting. Naming a stylistic device without explaining its function is not yet analysis.

es.b2.argumentation.title: Make a case
es.b2.argumentation.can_do: I can develop a balanced argument that weighs evidence and acknowledges objections.
es.b2.argumentation.guide: A developed argument weighs evidence and objections. Use aunque or si bien for concessions and por consiguiente for consequences. Aunque + indicative can present a fact accepted in the argument; aunque + subjunctive can present a hypothetical or non-asserted situation. Register matters: prefer precise claims to exaggerations such as siempre, nadie or todos when the evidence is limited.

es.b2.perspectives.title: Compare perspectives
es.b2.perspectives.can_do: I can compare viewpoints while separating attributed claims from my own inferences.
es.b2.perspectives.guide: When comparing perspectives, separate what each speaker says from what you infer. Use mientras que to contrast and ambos coinciden en que to state common ground. Attribute opinions clearly: según la autora; desde la perspectiva del entrevistado. Avoid presenting a person's experience as representative of an entire country, culture or group.

es.b2.exam-writing.title: Write with purpose
es.b2.exam-writing.can_do: I can plan and revise a formal response for its audience, purpose and text type.
es.b2.exam-writing.guide: Before writing, identify the task, recipient, purpose and required format. A formal email needs an appropriate greeting, a clearly stated request and a suitable closing. Revise content and organisation before polishing individual words. Check verb agreement, tense consistency, pronoun reference and written accents. A model answer illustrates one possible response; it is not a script to memorise.

es.tables.conditional.note: Add -ía endings to the whole infinitive. These forms express hypothetical actions and polite requests; context determines the meaning. Some verbs, such as poder and tener, use irregular stems.

es.a1.hay.rule: Hay means there is or there are. Its form does not change with number: hay un libro; hay tres libros. Introduce things with un/una, numbers or quantities. Use estar to locate something already identified: hay una biblioteca; la biblioteca está al lado del patio. No hay means there is not / there are no. Hay que + infinitive expresses a general obligation, without naming a person.

es.a1.ser-estar.rule.p1: Use ser for identity, origin, characteristics, time and the location of an event. Use estar for the location of people or things and for states. “Permanent versus temporary” is not a reliable rule: Madrid está en España; la reunión es en el aula.
es.a1.ser-estar.rule.p2: Some adjectives change meaning: es aburrido means boring; está aburrido means bored. Adjectives agree with the person or thing.
es.a1.present-regular.rule.p1: The presente describes habits and current situations. Remove -ar, -er or -ir and add the ending for the subject. The yo ending is -o in all three groups.
es.a1.present-regular.rule.p2: Nosotros and vosotros distinguish -er from -ir: comemos/coméis, vivimos/vivís. Subject pronouns can usually be omitted. An explicit time expression can also make the present refer to the future: mañana tenemos clase.
es.a1.present-stem.rule.p1: Some present-tense verbs change their stem in yo, tú, él/ella/usted and ellos/ellas/ustedes. Nosotros and vosotros keep the unchanged stem. Common patterns are pensar → pienso (e → ie), poder → puedo (o → ue) and pedir → pido (e → i).
es.a1.present-stem.rule.p2: Jugar changes u → ue: juego, but jugamos. The regular person endings remain. Do not apply these patterns to every verb with the same vowel: aprender is regular.
es.a1.present-irregular.rule.p1: Learn frequent irregular present forms as patterns. Ir is voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van. Several verbs have an irregular yo form: hago, tengo, salgo, pongo, digo, vengo.
es.a1.present-irregular.rule.p2: Some also change their stem in other persons: tengo/tienes/tenemos; digo/dices/decimos. Saber gives sé in yo, while conocer gives conozco. Ir a + infinitive expresses a plan; tener que + infinitive expresses a personal obligation.
es.a2.indefinido.rule.p1: The pretérito indefinido presents a past event as a complete whole: ayer visité el museo. It often advances a narrative. Regular -ar verbs use -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron; -er/-ir use -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron.
es.a2.indefinido.rule.p2: Keep the written accents: hablo and habló are different forms. Ir and ser share fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron. Other common forms include tuve, estuve, hice/hizo, pude and dije.
es.a2.indefinido.rule.p3: The imperfecto describes background or repeated past situations: llovía cuando llegamos. A long event can still use indefinido if presented as finished: estudié tres horas.
es.a2.imperfecto.rule.p1: Use the imperfecto to present a past situation from within, without focusing on its endpoint: habits, descriptions, ages and ongoing background. Regular -ar verbs use -aba; -er/-ir use -ía, with person endings. The main irregular verbs are ser (era), ir (iba) and ver (veía).
es.a2.imperfecto.rule.p2: The indefinido presents a completed event: mientras estudiaba, sonó el teléfono. Duration alone does not choose the tense: estudié dos horas is a completed block; estudiaba cuando llegaste gives background. Often several descriptions form the setting before the story moves on.
es.a2.perfecto.rule.p1: Build the pretérito perfecto compuesto with present haber + a past participle. Regular participles end in -ado (-ar) or -ido (-er/-ir). The participle does not agree with the subject: ella ha estudiado; ellas han estudiado.
es.a2.perfecto.rule.p2: Frequent irregular participles include hecho, visto, escrito, abierto, puesto and vuelto. This tense often connects a completed event to the present. In much of Spain it is common with hoy or esta semana; many American varieties also use the indefinido there.
es.a2.perfecto.rule.p3: Time words alone do not make every alternative wrong. These exercises explicitly request the perfecto when form choice is being tested.
es.a2.pronouns.rule.p1: Subject pronouns say who acts: yo, tú, él/ella/usted, nosotros/as, vosotros/as, ellos/ellas/ustedes. They are often omitted because the verb identifies the person. Direct-object pronouns replace what or whom the action directly affects: leo el libro → lo leo; veo a Ana → la veo.
es.a2.pronouns.rule.p2: Indirect-object pronouns identify the recipient: doy el libro a Ana → le doy el libro. Combine indirect before direct; le/les become se before lo/la/los/las: se lo doy. Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject: me levanto.
es.a2.pronouns.rule.p3: Pronouns normally precede a conjugated verb, but can attach to an infinitive: lo voy a leer / voy a leerlo. This course practises the general lo/la system; some accepted regional uses of le also exist.
es.b1.subjuntivo.rule.p1: The subjuntivo is a mood, not simply another past or future tense. Start with the presente de subjuntivo. It often appears after a wish, evaluation or doubt: quiero que vengas; es importante que estudies; no creo que sea fácil.
es.b1.subjuntivo.rule.p2: Affirming a belief normally takes indicative: creo que es fácil. For regular verbs, use the present yo stem and swap the vowel: hablar → hable; comer → coma; vivir → viva. Common irregular forms include sea, esté, vaya, haya, sepa and dé.
es.b1.subjuntivo.rule.p3: Nosotros/vosotros can behave differently with -ir stem changes: pedir → pidamos; dormir → durmamos. Same-subject wishes normally use an infinitive: quiero estudiar. With a different subject: quiero que estudies.
